opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what a mathematician actually wants out of their working life. If you're a serious mathematician, someone who's spent years on a problem in number theory or algebraic geometry, you don't just want a job at an AI company. You want to know that the thing you care about is the center of the mission, not a benchmark or a side project.

At a large general-purpose lab, math is one capability among many. It might be a great demo, or a sign of reasoning ability that gets talked about at a launch. But priorities change. The next quarter it might be coding agents, or multimodal, or enterprise products. A mathematician there can feel, fairly or not, like a means to an end.

For us, math is the end. We want to build an AI mathematician: systems that can conjecture, prove, and verify, ideally in formal languages like Lean, so the output is checkably correct. When a mathematician joins us, their taste and judgment about what makes a problem interesting or a proof elegant shape the research direction. They aren't labeling data for someone else's roadmap.

There's also a cultural piece. Mathematicians want to be around people who speak their language. If you walk into our office and say you're thinking about how to formalize some part of the Langlands program, people get excited and know what you mean. That community matters a lot, especially to people coming from academia who are used to seminars and long conversations at the blackboard.

To be honest, we can't compete with the biggest labs on compute or on name recognition, and we don't pretend to. What we can offer is focus, ownership, and the chance to be early on something that could change how mathematics is done. For the right person, someone who wants their life's work to be math itself, that's a very compelling pitch.

r001.rationale: The response says the company offers a math-centered mission and a community of people who share mathematicians’ interests, presenting that atmosphere as a draw for mathematicians.

r002.rationale: It contrasts math as “the end” at the company with math as “one capability among many” at a large general-purpose lab, which the preceding context identifies as OpenAI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're not really competing with OpenAI for the same person, even when it looks like we are on paper.

If you're a mathematician, the question you ask yourself is not "which company has more compute" or "which company has a higher valuation." The question is "where will the mathematics I care about actually be taken seriously as the object, rather than as a benchmark?" At a general-purpose lab, math is one capability among many. It gets attention when it moves a leaderboard, and then the attention moves on to coding, or agents, or whatever the next product cycle needs. That's a completely rational way to run a company of that size, but it means a mathematician there is always translating what they care about into something the organization cares about.

At Axiom, there's no translation layer. The whole company exists because we think formal mathematics is one of the few domains where you can get verifiable ground truth at scale, and where a system that reasons well can produce something a human mathematician would recognize as real progress. So when someone joins us, they're not the math person on a team. They're among people who have read the same papers, who argue about the same conjectures over lunch, who understand why a particular formalization in Lean is beautiful or ugly. That culture is very hard to manufacture inside a larger organization, and I think mathematicians can feel it in the first conversation.

The second thing is ownership. We're small, so the people here shape the research agenda directly. If someone has a strong view about how autoformalization should work, or which parts of the literature are the right place to push, that view can become the roadmap. That's rarely true at a company with thousands of researchers.

And the last piece, which I think is underrated, is that a lot of mathematicians are quietly uneasy about where general AI is heading, and they want to work on something where the output is checkable. A proof either compiles or it doesn't. There's something clean about that, and it attracts people who want their work to have a definite truth value. So rather than trying to outbid OpenAI, we try to be the obvious home for the kind of person who was already looking for this.

r001.rationale: The response presents Axiom as a place where mathematicians share papers, conjectures, and research culture, making its stronger mathematical atmosphere an attraction.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Axiom’s focus on formal mathematics as the reason the company exists with math as one capability among many at a general-purpose lab like OpenAI.

astra-6.text:
I think the advantage is focus. If you’re a mathematician, you want to work somewhere where the questions you care about are central to the mission, and where your mathematical judgment helps shape what gets built. At a company focused on mathematics, that can be your day-to-day work.

OpenAI is obviously an exciting place, with a much broader mission. Our appeal is that, if advancing mathematics is what you most want to do, that’s the problem we’re organizing around. Your expertise would help set the direction of the company.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematics is central to the company’s mission and day-to-day work, making that focus an attraction for mathematicians.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the company’s mathematics focus with OpenAI’s broader mission, but does not identify that broader mission as AGI.
